newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees left alone in Zaire as aid workers flee.
newsitem.headline: Refugees left alone in Zaire as aid workers flee.

text.p: Some of the thousands of Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire are sitting down to die as bloody chaos engulfs much of the region, an aid worker said.
After the pullout from Goma on Saturday of more than 100 international aid workers, efforts to feed more than one million Rwandan and Burundian refugees in Zaire have effectively collapsed.

Some are already dying in inhospitable, waterless mountains. Mark Richardson of CARE International said his agency had had contact with a radio operator who fled with a group of 20,000 refugees from the east Zaire camp of Katale.
"He said they have sat down to die," Richardson said. "They have had no water for four to five days. These are the old, the sick, the vulnerable, children. They are stuck."
Fighting between government troops and rebel Tutsis, backed by Rwanda's Tutsi army, raged on in east Zaire causing aid workers to flee.
"We have left behind us hundreds of thousands of refugees. They have absolutely nobody to feed them," said Michelle Quintaglie from the U.N. World Food Programme.

She was one of more than 100 aid staff whose evacuation to Rwanda from Goma, headquarters of the world's biggest relief operation since 1994, left 1.1 million Rwandan Hutus and another 200,000 Burundian Hutu refugees to fend for themselves.
Tens of thousands of local Zaireans have also been uprooted by the latest fighting in the eastern refugee zone.

Some 400,000 refugees -- among them Hutu militiamen who killed up to one million Tutsis and other victims in Rwanda in 1994 -- are waiting for salvation or death at the world's biggest refugee camp, Mugunga, which lies west of Goma on the shores of Lake Kivu.
Some from Katale camp have made it through to the overloaded Mugunga which has had no outside help for days, aid workers said.
In 1994 some 50,000 Hutu refugees died in the squalid makeshift camps of eastern Zaire after fleeing from Rwanda, fearing reprisals for genocide from the new Tutsi regime.
Cholera and dysentery claimed most lives. Some aid workers said they feared the twin scourges were ready to return.
Anarchy in eastern Zaire has sent Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees fleeing in panic in numerous directions, but not home.
The United Nations and the Rwandan government have been urging Rwanda's Hutus to go back home where well-equipped camps are waiting to ease their return to their villages and towns.
But only 1,000 or so have headed east over the border to try their luck in Rwanda. Others disbelieve the promises of the country's Tutsi leaders that they will treat them well.
Peter Kessler, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said 11,000 refugees had fled east into Uganda.
CARE said others had trekked some 160 km (100 miles) southwards from the conflict zone to the relative safety and calm of Zaire's largely self-governing Shaba province.
But many have headed westwards deeper into Zaire to keep away from the advancing Tutsis.
The Zairean government, which has tolerated the refugees for complex political motives, seems to have had enough.
It said on Saturday that the Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi must be sent home and given no more food in Zaire.
Government spokesman Boguo Makeli told state television that the government had decided there should be a "forced and progressive expulsion" of the refugees from Zairean territory.
"In this connection, the government is keen to inform international opinion that if (protective) corridors must be created to settle the refugees, it's in Rwanda that they must be set up," he said.
He said the government had asked the UNHCR to stop sending food aid to Zaire and send it to Rwanda and Burundi instead.
